Title: FORGE Lab uses agentic tools to identify memory safety issues in Rust
Context: For issue #161018, our testing found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions examined, and we assessed practical exploitation as unlikely
Full Text:
In this article

How we found and validated the bugs

Pattern 1: Trusting code not to panic

Pattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correct

Pattern 3: Trusting the underlying system

Why Rust still matters and advancing vulnerability discovery with AI

Rust's high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping

Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent.

Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly important as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day. Billions of people are estimated to interact with Rust-based software or operating systems daily, often without knowing it. Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript, GitHub rewrote the Copilot agent runtime in Rust, and Bun, Android, the Linux kernel, and Cloudflare are moving code to it as well. Much of this software relies on Rust’s foundational libraries, core and std, and the safety guarantees of the APIs they provide. Bugs in those libraries can have consequences well beyond the code where they originate.

Unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra, a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today.

In this post, we share some of the bugs we reported to the Rust issue tracker. We use them to discuss what Rust does and doesn’t guarantee, why writing correct unsafe Rust is so difficult, and why Rust’s safety model still matters even though its memory safety isn’t perfect.[OW1] [YB2]

How we found and validated the bugs

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we study vulnerabilities in complex software, including the Rust standard library. Our team combines years of experience in vulnerability research with AI-assisted tools that help us investigate code and find bugs that are difficult to uncover through traditional analysis alone.

Some of the bugs in this post were found with help from Hyenas, our research version of codename MDASH. Our researchers investigated the underlying code, reproduced the bugs, assessed their potential security impact, and worked with Rust maintainers to report and fix them.

This post focuses on soundness bugs in the standard library’s unsafe code. Bugs in the compiler itself, such as miscompilations and holes in the type system, are a different topic that we don’t cover here.

A note on open issues

At publication, two of the issues reported by our team remain open. The article also references related issues reported by others and fixes that are still under review. The Rust maintainers triaged and responded to our reports quickly, and we believe maintainers and the contributors working on these issues are doing their best and making the right tradeoffs among the many bugs they handle.

If you’re interested in an open issue, please comment only when you have something genuinely new to contribute, such as new information or an affected real-world use case.

Patterns of Rust’s Safety Bugs

At the lowest level, Rust uses unsafe blocks to work with raw pointers and interact directly with the operating system. Much of the standard library, including Vec and String, is built from small unsafe pieces wrapped in safe APIs. Inside an unsafe block, the programmer takes responsibility for the guarantees the compiler can’t check, and that responsibility extends to the safe API built around it. That API must be sound: no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.

Upholding that promise is harder than it looks. Consider a function that returns the byte at idx from any type that can be viewed as a byte slice, skipping the redundant bounds check after doing its own:

pub fn get>(s: &S, idx: usize) -> Option { if idx < s.as_ref().len() { // SAFETY: we just checked that `idx` is in bounds. Some(unsafe { *s.as_ref().get_unchecked(idx) }) } else { None } }

The hard part of unsafe Rust is knowing what you can trust. The function above looks correct, but it assumes that two calls to as_ref return the same slice. Because S is chosen by the caller, a safe AsRef implementation can return a long slice the first time and an empty one the second, and get reads out of bounds. Unsafe code must be careful with every call it makes, and the bugs we found fall into three patterns of misplaced trust: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Pattern 1: Trusting code not to panic

Unsafe code often breaks an invariant for a moment and restores it afterward; for example, it may allocate an uninitialized buffer and fill it directly, avoiding redundant writes to zero the memory first. That’s fine as long as the function runs to the end. But many operations in Rust can panic, from out-of-bounds indexing to calls into user-provided code, and by default a panic unwinds: it leaves the function early while still running destructors. Unwinding inside that window becomes an invisible exit that exposes the broken invariant to code that trusts it. Bugs of this kind are called panic safety bugs.

Figure 1 — Panic Safety.

MapWindows::clone (issue #156501)

We identified a panic safety issue in MapWindows::clone. The nightly API Iterator::map_windows yields overlapping windows of N items. It keeps the current window in a Buffer whose destructor drops the N items starting at start. In Rust 1.97.0, library/core/src/iter/adapters/map_windows.rs defines it as:

struct Buffer { // Invariant: `self.buffer[self.start..self.start + N]` is initialized, // with all other elements being uninitialized. This also // implies that `self.start <= N`. buffer: [[MaybeUninit; N]; 2], start: usize, }

Buffer::clone, in the same file, built the new buffer first and filled it afterward:

impl Clone for Buffer { fn clone(&self) -> Self { let mut buffer = Buffer { buffer: [[const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N], [const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N]], start: self.start, }; buffer.as_uninit_array_mut().write(self.as_array_ref().clone()); buffer } }

After buffer is constructed, it breaks its own invariant: its slots are uninitialized, but its destructor is already armed. The self.as_array_ref().clone() call runs the user's T::clone before the slots are written. If that call panics, unwinding drops buffer and runs drop_in_place on N uninitialized values. Our proof of concept uses only safe code: an element type whose clone always panics, which causes a crash when the destructor accesses uninitialized memory. The fix holds the new buffer in ManuallyDrop until it is fully written, so unwinding leaks the half-built buffer instead of dropping it.

The general lesson is to treat every call to code you don’t control, such as clone, drop, comparisons, closures, and iterator methods, as a possible early exit. Either finish the work that may panic before breaking an invariant, or make the broken state safe to unwind through: hold it in ManuallyDrop, or use a guard whose destructor restores the invariant, like Vec’s internal SetLenOnDrop. The Rustonomicon covers this under exception safety.

Allocators must not unwind

The recently stabilized Allocator API shows how hard panic safety is to get right. With std, an allocation failure aborts the process by default instead of unwinding, so much of the standard library's unsafe code assumes allocation never unwinds. Custom allocators can break that assumption. While the API was being stabilized, we reported one place in BTreeMap::insert that becomes unsound when an allocator unwinds, and others reported more (#159334, #159368, #159370). Fixing them one by one would mean auditing everything that allocates, so the stabilization, shipping in Rust 1.100 on November 12, instead requires implementors never to unwind from the trait's methods or from drop. The proposal notes that "unwinding out of many allocation-related methods was found to be a pervasive source of unsoundness."

Pattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correct

Unsafe code often calls into code its caller provides: a comparator, a trait implementation, a closure. That code is safe, but safe doesn’t mean correct, and it can return inconsistent or plainly wrong answers. The question is who is responsible when it does. In C++, it’s the caller. std::sort requires its comparator to be a strict weak ordering, and breaking that rule is undefined behavior. With libstdc++, sorting equal elements with <= reads past the end of the vector:

std::vector v(100, 42); // Bug: `<=` is not a strict weak ordering, since cmp(a, a) is true. std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; }); // AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow in std::__introsort_loop

The same comparator passed to Rust's sort_by is only a logic error. The sort may panic or leave the slice in an unspecified order, but it never causes undefined behavior. The responsibility sits with the unsafe code. The comparator is safe code supplied by the caller, so the unsafe code inside the sort must stay sound no matter what it returns. The same goes for every safe trait a user can implement: comparisons can be inconsistent, an ExactSizeIterator can report a length that doesn't match the items it yields, and Borrow can return a different value on each call.

str::replace with a custom Pattern (#156491)

Another of our bug reports shows how easy this trust is to miss: str::replace with a custom Pattern can create a non-UTF-8 String. String search APIs accept any type that implements the nightly Pattern trait, and a pattern can describe itself through as_utf8_pattern. str::replace uses that description to take a fast path when replacing one ASCII byte with another. In Rust 1.96.0, the fast path in library/alloc/src/str.rs looked like this:

pub fn replace(&self, from: P, to: &str) -> String { // Fast path for replacing a single ASCII character with another. if let Some(from_byte) = match from.as_utf8_pattern() { Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern([from_byte])) => Some(*from_byte), Some(Utf8Pattern::CharPattern(c)) => c.as_ascii().map(|ascii_char| ascii_char.to_u8()), _ => None, } { if let [to_byte] = to.as_bytes() { return unsafe { replace_ascii(self.as_bytes(), from_byte, *to_byte) }; } }

replace_ascii, in the same file, then rewrites the bytes:

unsafe fn replace_ascii(utf8_bytes: &[u8], from: u8, to: u8) -> String { let result: Vec = utf8_bytes.iter().map(|b| if *b == from { to } else { *b }).collect(); // SAFETY: We replaced ascii with ascii on valid utf8 strings. unsafe { String::from_utf8_unchecked(result) } }

The CharPattern branch checks that the character is ASCII, but the StringPattern branch assumes a one-byte string pattern must be ASCII. That holds for &str patterns, but StringPattern stored &[u8], and as_utf8_pattern is a safe method any Pattern can implement. In our proof of concept, a custom pattern reports the single byte 0x80, which only appears inside multibyte UTF-8 sequences:

impl Pattern for NonAsciiBytePattern { // ... fn as_utf8_pattern(&self) -> Option> { static NEEDLE: [u8; 1] = [0x80]; Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern(&NEEDLE)) } } // "\u{d000}" is [ed, 80, 80]; the result is [ed, 3f, 3f], which is not UTF-8. let corrupted = "\u{d000}".replace(NonAsciiBytePattern, "?");

str::replace rewrites the continuation bytes and returns a String that isn't valid UTF-8, and later string operations that rely on UTF-8 reach undefined behavior. The fix changed StringPattern to hold &str instead of &[u8], so the type itself now guarantees UTF-8.

When unsafe code depends on a property of a user-provided implementation, don’t take it on faith. Call the implementation once and keep the result, validate what it returns, or encode the property in a type that safe code can’t forge, as this fix did. If none of those work, make the trait unsafe so implementors explicitly promise to uphold it.

More examples

join shows how easy it is to fix this kind of bug only partway. In 2020, we reported that it trusted Borrow::borrow to return the same string on each call (CVE-2020-36323), and the fix handled strings that shrink between calls. In April 2026, the same function needed another fix: join borrows the first element twice, and if it grows on the second call, the remaining-length calculation underflows into a heap overflow. The earlier fix had never covered that path.

Others reported similar problems in the Pattern API this year. A safe Pattern can hand back a valid searcher built for a different string, and consumers such as strip_prefix_of apply its ranges to the original string unchecked, reading out of bounds (#158265). The same problem turned up in split_once (#165076) after a report that the Searcher contract doesn't spell out what str::split relies on (#164904). Both bugs are still open.

Pattern 3: Trusting the underlying system

The first two patterns stay inside Rust code. The third sits at the boundary with the operating system, where unsafe code trusts process-wide state such as signal stacks, memory mappings, and the environment, which other threads, C libraries, or the kernel can touch at any time. These bugs have been hard to find automatically, because a static analyzer would need to model all of that surrounding behavior. AI agents change the picture: they understand enough about the environment the code runs in to make this area practical to search. We started exploring it and found some interesting bugs.

process::exit and the main thread’s signal stack (#161018)

When a thread overflows its stack, Rust prints a clear message and aborts instead of crashing with a bare segmentation fault:

thread 'main' (3307186) has overflowed its stack fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting

This relies on a few pieces of process-wide state. Each thread’s stack ends in a guard page, an inaccessible region just past the stack’s limit: pthread reserves one for every spawned thread, and on Linux the kernel’s own stack guard plays that role for the main thread. Touching it raises SIGSEGV, and Rust registers a handler for that signal. The handler can’t run on the stack that just overflowed, so Rust also gives each thread an alternate signal stack, a small separate mapping with a guard page of its own, which the kernel switches to when it delivers the signal. The handler checks that the faulting address is inside the guard page, prints the message, and aborts.

Figure 2 — Stack Overflow.

We found that calling process::exit from a child thread tears down the main thread’s alternate stack while the main thread is still running. process::exit runs the runtime’s cleanup before calling libc’s exit, and in Rust 1.98.0 that cleanup ends in library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs:

pub unsafe fn cleanup() { if cfg!(panic = "immediate-abort") { return; } // FIXME: I probably cause more bugs than I'm worth! // see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/111272 unsafe { drop_handler(MAIN_ALTSTACK.load(Ordering::Relaxed)) }; }

The cleanup function passes MAIN_ALTSTACK, the main thread’s alternate stack, to drop_handler:

// SAFETY: we warned the caller this disables the alternate signal stack! unsafe { sigaltstack(&disabling_stack, ptr::null_mut()) }; // SAFETY: We know from `get_stackp` that the alternate stack we installed is part of // a mapping that started one page earlier, so walk back a page and unmap from there. unsafe { munmap(data.sub(page_size), sigstack_size + page_size) };

The call to sigaltstack disables the alternate stack of the calling thread, but the subsequent call to munmap unmaps the main thread’s. The code assumes it runs on the main thread, which isn’t true when a child thread calls process::exit. The main thread keeps running until libc’s exit finishes, with its signal stack registration still pointing at unmapped memory. If it overflows its stack in that window, the kernel can’t deliver the signal, and our proof of concept dies with a plain segmentation fault instead of Rust’s message. The bug dates back to 2015, and the fix stops cleaning up the main thread’s alternate stack altogether.

We also checked whether this could become a security issue. In theory, it could lead to code execution: if a writable mapping landed at the old alternate stack’s address, the kernel would deliver the main thread’s next signal onto it, and another thread could overwrite the handler’s frame, such as its return address, while it runs. In practice, the conditions are very tight. Everything has to happen in the brief window before libc’s exit finishes, the new mapping must have exactly the right size to reuse that address, and overwriting the frame takes a second race inside a short handler. For issue #161018, our testing found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions examined, and we assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. This assessment does not automatically apply to the other issues discussed. The issue has more details in its security impact analysis.

CommandExt::exec and the global environment (#156951)

Our other report involves the process environment. On Unix, CommandExt::exec replaces the current process with a new program. When the command has its own environment variables, exec points the process-global environ at a new array, calls execvp, and restores environ if execvp fails. In Rust 1.99.0, Command::exec takes the environment lock in library/std/src/sys/process/unix/unix.rs:

let _lock = sys::env::env_read_lock(); let Err(e) = self.do_exec(theirs, envp.as_ref());

Command::do_exec, in the same file, then swaps the environment:

_reset = Some(Reset(*sys::env::environ())); *sys::env::environ() = envp.as_ptr(); } libc::execvp(self.get_program_cstr().as_ptr(), self.get_argv().as_ptr()); Err(io::Error::last_os_error())

Command::exec takes only the read side of the environment lock, yet do_exec writes the process-global environ. Before the write, do_exec saves the old value so it can be restored if execvp fails. Writing environ under a read lock lets other threads in. A thread calling env::var takes the same read lock and can see variables meant only for the new program, and two failed exec calls racing each other can leave environ pointing at a freed array that a later env::vars_os() reads. Both proofs of concept use only safe Rust. A 2018 fix held an exclusive lock here, but when the environment lock became a read-write lock in 2021, exec kept the read side. A fix that avoids touching environ by calling execve directly is in review.

The environment has caused trouble before. After a discussion that began in 2015, the 2024 edition marked env::set_var as unsafe, because C functions on most Unix platforms read the environment without going through Rust's lock.

process::exit and thread-local destructors (#164243)

Getting this boundary right is hard, and more problems are still open. While exploring this area, we independently ran into a double free in safe code that process::exit can cause through thread-local destructors. It was reported by someone else (#164243), but it’s worth mentioning here. libc’s exit first runs the calling thread’s thread-local destructors, as C++ requires, and Rust registers its destructors the same way. If a destructor calls process::exit while a thread local is being replaced, libc drops that thread local a second time. A proposed fix switches process::exit to POSIX _exit, which ends the process without running these handlers.

Why Rust still matters and advancing vulnerability discovery with AI

Every unsafe block rests on assumptions about the code around it. The bugs in this post came from three kinds of misplaced trust:

that code won't panic at the wrong moment,

that a caller-provided implementation behaves correctly, and

that the process-wide state Rust shares with the operating system and the C library stays the way the code expects.

Familiar patterns are still difficult (Patterns 1 and 2)

The first two patterns are well studied. Rudra looked for both in 2021, and the standard library was already fixing panic safety bugs in 2015 (CVE-2015-20001). They remain challenging to avoid because any call inside unsafe code might unwind or run code the caller supplied.

What we saw this year was mixed. On the positive side, the nightly process is working. Many reports were caught while the affected APIs were still unstable, and several were fixed by changing the design before stabilization. StringPattern now holds &str instead of &[u8], and Allocator was stabilized with a rule that implementors must not unwind. At the same time, bugs in these patterns still reach stable releases, and their fixes aren't always complete. join was fixed in 2020 and needed another fix in 2026 for a path the first fix had missed.

System boundary bugs are now within reach (Pattern 3)

The third pattern is different. Its bugs live where Rust meets the layers below it: the kernel, through system calls such as sigaltstack and munmap, and the C library, through process-wide state such as environ and the cleanup that libc's exit runs. Getting them right takes knowledge that lives outside Rust's type system, which has made these bugs difficult to find with traditional static analysis. That may also be why they last so long. The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years, and exec has written environ under a read lock since 2021. Unlike our reports in the first two patterns, both affect stable Rust.

Language models already know a great deal about how these interfaces behave, so agentic scanners can check unsafe code against the system it runs on, not just the language. We think this boundary is one of the most promising places for agentic security research, in Rust and beyond.

Rust's high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping

Rust holds its safe APIs to a stricter standard than C and C++. Safe code must never be able to cause undefined behavior, no matter how it uses an API. In C++, a comparator that breaks std::sort's ordering requirement causes undefined behavior, while Rust's sort must stay memory-safe with any Ord implementation. POSIX doesn't guarantee that setenv is safe to call while another thread reads the environment. That makes memory safety bugs in Rust hard to compare one-to-one with bugs in other languages.

For the same reason, a soundness bug in the standard library isn't automatically a vulnerability in the programs that use it. Each bug in this post needs an unusual setup to trigger, such as a panic at exactly the wrong moment, a deliberately misbehaving implementation, or calling process::exit from a child thread. It becomes a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way.

Rust's safety standard is strict and difficult to meet, but it's also useful. It gives an unambiguous answer to what counts as a soundness bug, so problems can be fixed and prevented once in the library, instead of in every program that uses it. Rust's safety model strikes the right balance between control, safety, and performance for systems programming, which is why so many projects choose it.

Beyond the lab

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we're exploring how technology such as codename MDASH can help researchers find bugs like the ones in this post at greater scale. Rust's standard library is one of several foundational open source projects where we're applying this approach.

This research also extends beyond the lab. It helps inform the development of codename MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. These findings can also serve as inputs to Microsoft Perception, our new multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work together across broader security workflows. For example, the Web App Pen Test Agent can use codename MDASH findings to help prioritize testing, validate exploitability against live applications, and produce actionable vulnerabilities that downstream agents can use to prioritize and support remediation. This connects AI-powered code analysis with real-world security validation and response, helping security teams move from identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding and addressing actual risk.

Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs, it's to identify meaningful issues, turn those findings into actionable research, and improve the safety of foundational software that developers and organizations depend on.

In October 2026, the financially motivated threat actor Storm-3358 began targeting organizations in the financial sector using the agentic AI offensive framework ARTEX. The threat actor that Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks as Storm-3358 is a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia, in addition to a smaller number of large financial organizations globally.

Microsoft has observed Storm-3358 use ARTEX in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public internet, exploit security flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery (SSRF), and install open-source remote access trojans (RATs). Storm-3358 has used the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs for persistence and lateral movement. Microsoft has observed ARTEX agents using utilities like netcat and curl to download these RATs to compromised systems, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Example commands that ARTEX agents used to download RATs to compromised systems.

In recent ARTEX-related attacks, threat actors have used ARTEX agents to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in web applications, use web shells for persistence on compromised web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration. ARTEX agents can also perform brute-force password attacks, password spraying, API enumeration and abuse, and database dumping. Agentic tools like ARTEX can leverage compromised credentials and systems at machine speed to move laterally, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

While threat actors regularly use proxies and virtual private networks (VPNs) to change the source IP address of malicious traffic and bypass static detections, Microsoft is providing indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help defenders detect related activity.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft’s research into threats involving agentic frameworks informs security detections and investigative context across its products. The capabilities available to customers depend on the source of the activity and the products and protections deployed in their environment.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

For additional information on the evolution of threat actors’ use of ARTEX please see Microsoft’s recent blogs: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise and Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets.

Context: Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks...

In this article

From exposed secrets to cloud compromise

Follow-on actions

Mitigating application credential abuse activity

Defending against agentic AI attacks

Microsoft detections

Advanced hunting queries

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, including credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services. These threat actors can then use the secrets for further malicious activity against the compromised organization.

Searching open code repositories for exposed credentials, secrets, keys, and other authentication material is a well-documented technique that has historically been limited by the time required for human operators to find code repositories, review the data in the repositories, and leverage authentication material for further action. However, agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain. In at least one case, Microsoft observed an AI agent advance from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes.

Microsoft has also investigated follow-on activity involving the misuse of valid application credentials. As early as October 28, 2026, Microsoft began observing successful service principal sign-ins from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84 involving multiple application IDs across some impacted customers, including cases where a multitenant application credential was compromised at the source (vendor-owned application) and used to access multiple downstream tenants. The threat actor used the compromised credentials for cloud resource discovery, and credential and data exfiltration, including from Azure Key Vaults and Storage Accounts, and abuse of Azure AI services consistent with the activity described above. Additionally, Microsoft observed malicious activity originating from two IP addresses potentially associated with this campaign. We identified malicious operations from 65.87.223[.]26, including indications of vulnerability exploitation by embedded shell commands in a user agent and attempts to obtain App Service authentication tokens. A similar campaign involving the same IPs addressed was also reported by Todyl. Separately, Microsoft observed reconnaissance operations from 157.22.126[.]128 targeting AI workloads deployed by victims on Azure AI services.

Microsoft encourages organizations to scan their code in GitHub and determine where any secrets are present. In addition to removing the secrets from the code base, affected organizations should immediately rotate any exposed keys or credentials. GitHub monitors public repositories by automatically scanning for secrets. In addition to scanning their own repositories, organizations can enable public monitoring through GitHub to detect secrets leaked in secondary public repositories across GitHub. This extends secret scanning beyond the repositories an enterprise owns to follow potential secret exposure across the platform. GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps scans for credentials and other sensitive content in source code. Push protection can also block supported secrets before they’re pushed. Organizations need either GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps or, for organizations using the standalone experience, GitHub Secret Protection for Azure DevOps enabled.

Secrets are exposed in public repositories when code containing the secret is committed to GitHub. Developers might store secrets in configuration files, scripts, or other code to quickly operationalize the OAuth application or avoid configuring more modern authentication flows. Organizations can reduce exposure by protecting workload identities and secrets, enforcing least privilege, safeguarding recovery resources, and enabling relevant Microsoft Defender for Cloud protections. Publicly exposed credentials remain usable until revoked or rotated; removing the original disclosure alone does not remediate the exposure. Microsoft recommends that developers migrate OAuth applications away from secret-based authentication. While storing long-lived application client secrets in code is a common practice, using managed identities for application authentication eliminates the possibility of secret exposure in code, manual processes associated with secret management, and barriers to securely scaling applications.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

From exposed secrets to cloud compromise

Starting in August 2026, Microsoft observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to submit large volumes of queries to GitHub for secrets. The queries submitted by the AI framework often included the name of a target organization, keywords for secrets, a keyword linked to cloud services, or a keyword linked to another AI service provider. Organizations that find their secrets exposed in public repositories must assume that the exposed secrets and associated applications are compromised.

Follow-on actions

Credential abuse via Entra ID

In one follow-on attack that began as early as October 28, 2026, an agentic framework used valid leaked or stolen application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants of certain organizations and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. The sign-ins primarily came from two IP addresses: 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18. The latter IP address is a Tor exit node, which might be associated with unrelated malicious activity, including from unrelated sources. The agent successfully conducted service principal sign-ins on dozens of associated applications across multiple tenants.. Service principals are the identities that applications use to authenticate and give direct, programmatic access to whatever the application is authorized to reach.

The threat actor targeted operations that return credentials, including storage account keys, App Service settings, connection strings and publishing credentials, AI and machine learning (ML) connections and datastores, and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) user credentials. The compromised applications subsequently accessed SharePoint and OneDrive in the targeted organization tenants, including file downloads and mailbox-item access. In some tenants, the threat actor sent Microsoft Graph API requests, which were mostly searches to find content of interest. The threat actor enumerated subscriptions, resource groups, permissions, AI model deployments, and service configurations in Azure to map the environment.

Additionally, the threat actor attempted to validate stolen Azure resources, including compromised Azure AI services, as identified using Defender for Cloud’s AI threat protection. Observed activity suggests that the threat actor might have attempted to abuse some of these compromised AI resources to facilitate their broader attack activity.

Figure 1. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed across the credential abuse attack chain

Cloud API adjustments indicative of adaptive behavior

Additionally in this attack the agent’s operations on a victim’s Azure Resource Manager (ARM) instance originating from 199.19.77[.]84 demonstrated sequences consistent with adaptive troubleshooting, where failed cloud API requests were followed by changes to HTTP methods or API versions and subsequent HTTP 200 responses:

A batch of ARM requests attempting to enumerate secret metadata across multiple Azure Key Vault resources returned HTTP 400 (Bad Request). These requests specified a version associated with Key Vault’s data-plane APIs against ARM (control-plane) APIs. Approximately 28 seconds after the first failed response, a batch rerun began against the same vault resource paths using the ARM API version 2023-07-01 and returned HTTP 200.

A GET request to enumerate an Azure SQL server’s firewall rules specified an outdated API version and returned HTTP 400. Approximately 60 seconds after that request, a matching GET began using a supported version and subsequently returned HTTP 200. The URL changed only in its api-version parameter.

An ARM POST request to an Application Insights query endpoint returned HTTP 400 because an outdated API version was specified. Approximately 80 seconds after the failed request, another POST began against the same endpoint, specifying a supported API version, and subsequently returned HTTP 200.

OAuth application abuse

In multiple cases, Microsoft observed the same agentic AI tools subsequently obtain a token for a single-tenant OAuth application in the same target organization, then use the compromised OAuth application to enumerate other cloud resources within the organization. In some cases, the agents exfiltrated secrets from the organization’s Azure Key Vault. The agents once authenticated have also searched Azure DevOps for secrets. Until the secrets are revoked or rotated, they can allow a threat actor to maintain persistence in the organization, compromise additional identities, or hijack resources. In one observed case, an AI agent progressed from searching for the client secrets in GitHub to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

The agents also used the compromised OAuth application to use the Run Command, which runs scripts in Azure VMs. With access to this functionality on a VM, a threat actor can access unsecured credentials and other stored data, compromise associated workload identities, or run code that provides persistence or lateral movement.

During this activity, the AI agents repeatedly demonstrated a focus on credentials that provide access to AI services, such as API keys for major AI service providers and OAuth applications with access to Foundry Tools (previously known as Azure Cognitive Services). Multiple public reports have documented threat actors using agentic AI tools to compromise credentials for AI services, sometimes to run the same agentic AI workflow.

Mitigating application credential abuse activity

Microsoft recommends the following mitigation steps to contain, detect, and investigate this threat.

Containment

Block 199.19.77[.]84/32 as a named location in a Conditional Access policy targeting workload identities, assigned directly to service principals, and in a user-scoped block policy to cover replayed sessions. Note that workload identity policies require Workload ID Premium licensing and cover only single-tenant apps registered in your tenant. Block the exact IP rather than the whole ASN.

For affected users, revoke Entra sessions, Azure DevOps PATs and SSH keys.

For any affected application, remove all client secrets, certificates and federated credentials, including those added by the threat actor and disable the service principal if needed. Tokens already issued remain valid until expiry.

Rotate everything stored in any Key Vault the affected application could read, and any credentials found in accessed documents.

MSPs: Review Partner Center access, GDAP relationships, and customer tenants, and notify affected customers per your agreements.

Detection and hunting

Review Entra service principal and non-interactive sign-in logs for 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18 including failed attempts. Sign-in errors AADSTS7000215 (invalid secret) or AADSTS7000222 (expired secret) indicate someone holds a credential for your app; a failure followed by a success is urgent.

Review Azure Activity, Key Vault and Storage diagnostics, Entra audit, Azure DevOps audit and Microsoft 365 unified audit logs for the address, including secret reads, blob and file downloads, and changes to apps, permissions or pipelines.

In Azure DevOps auditing, review PAT creation and first use, federated service connections, pipeline runs and edits, and unfamiliar user agents. Enable auditing if it is off.

Look for behavior as well as the IP: one address authenticating to three or more service principals with mixed success, or one app requesting tokens across Azure Resource Manager, Key Vault, Storage and Graph in a short window. Search as far back as retention allows.

Defending against agentic AI attacks

Threat actors can and do change the source IP address, user agent strings, and other fingerprints left by the agentic AI penetration testing tools they use. This can make identifying and blocking malicious network traffic early difficult for defenders.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat.

Protect and continuously assess application credentials and secrets. Avoid storing service principal credentials, storage keys, connection strings, and other secrets in source code, configuration files, public repositories, issues, or other locations where they might be inadvertently exposed. To find credentials in source code, consider using tools like GitHub Advanced Security or other OWASP source code analysis tools.

Rotate compromised or exposed credentials immediately and establish credential lifecycle practices. Treat credentials that have been publicly exposed as compromised, even if the original location has subsequently been edited or deleted. Removing the content does not invalidate the credential or eliminate copies retained in edit history, caches, archives, logs, or other systems. Immediately revoke or rotate the affected credentials and investigate their historical use. Where supported, organizations should favor mechanisms that reduce reliance on long-lived credentials. Learn more about protecting secrets with Defender for Cloud.

Enable appropriate Microsoft Defender for Cloud plans for critical Azure workloads. Consider enabling workload protections relevant to the resources in your environment, including Defender for Resource Manager, Defender for Storage, Defender for Key Vault, Defender for App Service, and Defender for Databases. Learn more in the Microsoft Defender for Cloud overview.

Apply least privilege to service principals and other workload identities. Review the Azure role-based access control (RBAC) permissions assigned to service principals and restrict their privileges to the resources and operations required by their applications. Learn more about best practices for Azure RBAC.

Protect backup and recovery infrastructure as part of resilience. Restrict access to backup and recovery resources and closely monitor attempts to modify or remove their protection controls. Learn more about Azure Backup security best practices.

Hardening OAuth applications against compromise involves managing the permissions of the applications in your organization and securing application secrets. To triage applications in your environment, enforce security policies with new applications as they are created, and address existing applications over time beginning with the most recent ones.

Identify and catalog applications running in your cloud environment. The Cloud app catalog page in Defender for Cloud Apps is one service that can help accomplish this.

Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps Cloud Discovery tools to identify unmanaged apps, and prioritize the most frequently used apps to migrate and integrate.

Use Conditional Access policies for workload identities. Consider augmenting identity signals with workload identity risk protection.

Set permission restrictions to limit who can create an application in the tenant. This can be achieved by setting the ability for users to register apps to “No” and limiting the application developer role to privileged users. Review the list of least privileged roles by task to help scope role-based access control in your environment.

Integrate enterprise applications with Microsoft Entra ID.

Microsoft detections

Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog.

Advanced hunting queries

The following hunting queries are related to the October 28 Entra ID service principal sign-in activity.

Find successful and failed application sign-ins from the suspicious IP addresses

let startTime = datetime(2026-10-28T00:00:00Z); let endTime = now(); EntraIdSpnSignInEvents | where Timestamp between (startTime .. endTime) | where IPAddress in ("199.19.77.84") | project Timestamp, TenantId, Application, ApplicationId, ServicePrincipalName, ServicePrincipalId, ResourceDisplayName, ResourceId, ResourceTenantId, IPAddress, ErrorCode, UserAgent, CorrelationId, RequestId | order by Timestamp asc

Find Microsoft Graph API requests from the two IP addresses, including searches and response status

let startTime = datetime(2026-10-28T00:00:00Z); let endTime = now(); GraphAPIAuditEvents | where Timestamp between (startTime .. endTime) | where IpAddress in ("199.19.77.84") | project Timestamp, TenantId, ApplicationId, ServicePrincipalId, AccountObjectId, IpAddress, RequestMethod, RequestUri, ResponseStatusCode, ResponseSize, Scopes, EntityType, TargetWorkload, UniqueTokenIdentifier, ClientRequestId, OperationId, RequestId | order by Timestamp asc

Find available Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Azure cloud activity details from the suspicious IP addresses

let startTime = datetime(2026-10-28T00:00:00Z); let endTime = now(); CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp between (startTime .. endTime) | where IPAddress in ("199.19.77.84") | project Timestamp, Application, CloudAppId = ApplicationId, ActionType, ActivityType, AccountType, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, UserAgent, ObjectName, ObjectType, ObjectId, ActivityObjects, ReportId, RawEventData | order by Timestamp asc

CloudAuditEvents | where IPAddress has_any ('199.19.77.84','65.87.223.26')

Title: New investments to reduce on-premises security risk
Context: Since September 2026, Microsoft has released not only Critical but also Important security updates outside the traditional Patch Tuesday schedule when faster action is needed,...
Full Text:
On-premises servers can be essential to business operations, but they are increasingly attractive targets to attackers. AI can help less-skilled actors analyze software, develop malicious tools, and repeat attack workflows at greater speed and scale, shortening the window between exposure and exploitation. Organizations need to strengthen security faster without disrupting the critical workloads they rely on. Today, we’re announcing a new on-premises security initiative, initially focused on server workloads. The initiative brings together guidance, migration, and product investments to help customers understand and prioritize risk, reduce their on-premises footprint wherever possible, and strengthen critical workloads that need to remain. Guidance for the initiative will soon be available through Secure Now, which also includes our AI readiness checklist in Microsoft Security Exposure Management and guidance for strengthening foundational security.

Understand Identify the most important on-premises risks and prioritize actions customers can take now.

Reduce Move workloads to Microsoft 365 where possible to take advantage of cloud-based security, resilience, and continuous innovation.

Secure Strengthen critical workloads that need to remain on-premises and reduce the manual work required to keep them secure.

This approach starts with understanding where to focus—and extends to making supported on-premises products more secure by default.

Modernize where you can, and strengthen the security of what must remain.

Making supported on-premises workloads more secure by default

Within the Secure pillar of the on-premises security initiative, we’re also hardening the products themselves through On-Premises Baseline Security Mode, starting with supported Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server workloads.

On-Premises Baseline Security Mode

On-Premises Baseline Security Mode is designed to make the default security posture stronger—reducing the number of recommended security settings administrators must configure and maintain manually. For supported on-premises server workloads, it starts with a validated and tested secure-by-default configuration from initial deployment, while preserving administrator control. Building on protections available today, it progressively establishes and maintains more of the recommended security posture through the products themselves, adapting the baseline as threats and Microsoft security guidance evolve.

The result is less manual effort and a stronger security posture maintained increasingly through the products themselves. We’re advancing this work across three areas: Patch, Configure, and Protect.

Figure 1: On-Premises Baseline Security Mode builds on capabilities available today across Patch, Configure, and Protect, with greater automation and stronger defaults coming over time.

Patch: close known vulnerabilities faster

The need is clear in our deployment data: many Exchange Server deployments are not running the current security update, including a substantial share on unsupported versions. Closing this protection gap requires both releasing fixes faster and helping customers apply them sooner.

Today. Since September 2026, Microsoft has released not only Critical but also Important security updates outside the traditional Patch Tuesday schedule when faster action is needed, helping customers address known vulnerabilities sooner.

Next. In Q1 calendar year 2027, we’re targeting automatic application of security updates after a fixed period following release in connected SharePoint Server, Exchange Server, and Skype for Business Server environments.

Release fixes faster, then help those fixes reach servers faster.

Configure: make the safer posture easier to maintain

Security requires more than current software. Configuration and permissions can drift over time, creating gaps between the intended security posture and the environment administrators are operating. Customers need a clearer way to identify those gaps, establish recommended settings, and maintain them as environments evolve.

Today. Tenant Configuration Management can help customers assess supported SharePoint, Exchange, and Skype for Business Server environments and identify where permissions are broader than intended.

Next. In Q1 2027, we plan to introduce hardened default configurations for SharePoint Server, Exchange Server, and Skype for Business Server, moving from identifying configuration risk toward establishing Microsoft-recommended security settings by default. We also plan to identify configuration drift so administrators can see when environments move away from that baseline.

Make the safer configuration easier to establish and harder to unintentionally lose.

Protect: reduce exposure when threats can’t wait for a patch

Some threats emerge before a permanent security update is available and fully deployed. During that window, customers need mitigations that can reduce exposure quickly without replacing the underlying security update.

Today. Emergency Mitigation Service can automatically apply interim mitigations for certain emerging vulnerabilities, helping reduce exposure while a permanent security update is prepared and deployed. Mitigation addresses the immediate risk; the security update addresses the underlying vulnerability.

Next. In December 2026, we plan to introduce Emergency Mitigation Service 2.0 for Exchange Server and Skype for Business Server, enabling it by default and expanding the security mitigations it can apply. In January 2027, we are planning to extend Emergency Mitigation Service 2.0 to cover SharePoint Server.

When threats move faster, protection needs to move faster too.

Act today, prepare for what comes next

Taken together, these investments represent an important shift: from providing customers with security guidance and tools toward building the recommended security posture into the products themselves.

Microsoft continues to recommend moving workloads to Microsoft 365 wherever possible. Start by identifying which workloads can move and which must remain on-premises. For those that remain, move to supported releases, assess exposure, apply current security updates, and enable available protections.

The Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server teams will publish additional guidance on available protections, upcoming capabilities, and actions customers can take now. We also plan to bring practitioner-focused on-premises guidance to Secure Now to help organizations assess their environment, identify critical actions, and prioritize the steps they can take.

Join us at Microsoft Ignite for Secure your on-prem estate (BRK215) to explore the initiative, upcoming investments, and steps you can take now.

Modernize where you can. Strengthen the security of what must remain.

Title: ​​​​What’s new in Microsoft Security: November 2026
Context: Now generally available, Defender discovers more than 50 supported local AI agents by observing their activity and brings the agent, device, account, and configured MCP context...
Full Text:
Endpoint administrators need to keep elevated access accountable at scale. Security teams also need a clearer view of expert-led protection and a simpler way to deploy SQL Server protection in Azure Government. As AI agents gain access to business data and tools, organizations need ways to limit their authority and adapt protection as risk changes. This month’s Microsoft Intune and Microsoft Defender updates introduce capabilities across these areas, alongside new Secure AI capabilities for agent access. A recent Secure Now update in Microsoft Security Exposure Management also connects information on recent threats to focused initiatives for reducing exposure.

Here’s what’s new:

Limit agent authority to the task with Dynamic Permissions

Give agents task-scoped authority and adapt access as risk changes

As agents gain access to business data and tools, organizations need ways to manage what each agent is allowed to do. Dynamic Permissions provides an agent its own permissions and authority, scoped to its current task and for only as long as the task requires. As the agent works, Dynamic Agent Risk assesses whether the agent’s authority aligns with changing behavior and context. Dynamic Conditional Access can then respond proportionately by narrowing permissions, restricting access to resources, or requiring human approval for higher-impact actions. Together, these capabilities are designed to help organizations tailor agent authority before an agent acts and adjust access as risk changes. See how security can respond when an agent steps outside its task.

Contain local AI agents with Microsoft Execution Containers

Apply least-privilege boundaries to help limit access on Windows

Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), now generally available, gives organizations an operating system-enforced containment layer for AI agents, designed to limit what an agent can access. Rather than relying on the agent to behave within intended boundaries, MXC applies least-privilege controls across files, networks, processes, and user interactions, with additional isolation options for higher-risk scenarios. Organizations can tune and validate policies before enforcing them broadly, while upcoming integration with Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Entra, and Microsoft Agent 365 is intended to extend governance and attribution across the enterprise. Discover more about this policy-driven containment for AI agents.

Scale least privilege with Microsoft Intune Endpoint Privilege Management

Expand least-privilege scenarios with new system settings support and simpler tenant onboarding

Microsoft Intune Endpoint Privilege Management continues to expand the tasks standard users can complete without broad administrator rights. With new system settings support, standard users can change IPv4, IPv6, and DNS server values on their device’s network adapters through Endpoint Privilege Management, while administrators determine how those changes are elevated. For user-confirmed changes, administrators can require a business justification, Windows authentication, or both before the change is applied. Along with tenant onboarding updates, these improvements support organizations as they get started with and expand their use of Endpoint Privilege Management. Explore how to get started with system settings support in Endpoint Privilege Management.

Get started with Microsoft Intune Endpoint Privilege Management

Simplify security operations with Defender Experts

See what Defender Experts are investigating in a consolidated experience

As threats move faster and security environments grow more complex, security teams need to quickly understand what matters and when to act. New Microsoft Defender Experts MDR experiences in the Microsoft Defender portal bring ongoing expert work into focus with a consolidated overview page with updated navigation and visibility into hunts. Teams can review active and completed hunts, see findings from Defender Experts, and identify items that may require follow-up. Learn more about the new Defender Experts MDR experiences.

Get around-the-clock defense with Microsoft Defender Experts MDR

Extend protection and discover local agents with Microsoft Defender

Simplify deployment and expand SQL protection

The enhanced agent for Defender for SQL Servers on machines is now generally available for resource- and subscription-level enablement in Azure Government cloud. The enhanced agent uses existing SQL infrastructure, eliminating the need to deploy the Azure Monitor Agent for this scenario. Security teams can spend less time on deployment and extend protection across their SQL Server environments. Learn more about the enhanced agent and how to get started.

Discover local AI agents and their configured MCPs on Windows and macOS

On endpoints, Microsoft Defender is extending discovery capabilities for supported local AI agents and their configured model context protocols (MCPs) across Windows and macOS. Now generally available, Defender discovers more than 50 supported local AI agents by observing their activity and brings the agent, device, account, and configured MCP context together to help security teams understand local AI agent activity in their environment. Learn more about local agents.

Explore Microsoft Defender solutions

Improve security posture with Microsoft Security Exposure Management

Prioritize foundational security controls with Secure Now

AI-enabled attacks can take advantage of familiar weaknesses, including excessive permissions, unprotected authentication flows, and exposed systems. Secure Now now pairs information about recent threats with focused initiatives across security domains. Security teams can use that context to identify foundational controls that need attention, review the recommended actions, and prioritize work intended to reduce exposure. The update helps connect information about observed attack patterns with security improvements teams can consider in their own environments.

Learn more about Microsoft Security Exposure Management

Learn how to address agentic AI’s security challenges

From agentic inventory and observability to stopping AI runtime threats

An inventory is only the starting point for managing Al agent risk. Organizations also need to consider ownership, limits on what agents can access, how risk is reassessed as agents operate, and protections against emerging threats. “Don’t Leave AI Exposed” provides security professionals, IT administrators, and developers with actionable guidance on managing risk across the agent lifecycle. Download the guide for considerations spanning agent inventory, ownership, access, monitoring, and runtime protection.

Stay in the Loop

Security teams need a clear account of what is changing across the portfolio and where those changes can strengthen their operations. In the Loop brings together the latest Microsoft Security updates and their implications for your security strategy. Explore earlier editions and check back for the next drop.

See Microsoft Security innovations in action at Microsoft Ignite, November 17-20, 2026, in San Francisco or online.

To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn (Microsoft Security) and X (@MSFTSecurity) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity.
